questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a new parent about umbilical cord care for their newborn. Which instruction is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sponge-bathed rather than fully submerged, until the cord stump has completely separated on its own","B":"Covered loosely with a breathable dressing until the stump shows early signs of detachment","C":"Keep the cord stump clean and dry, allowing it to air dry, and fold diapers below the cord to avoid irritation","D":"Left in place until it separates on its own, with gentle traction applied only if it appears nearly detached"}}
questions.rationale: Standard newborn cord care involves keeping the stump clean and dry, allowing air exposure, avoiding submersion baths until the cord falls off naturally (typically 1-3 weeks), and folding diapers below the stump to prevent irritation and contamination, allowing natural separation.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Newborn Umbilical Cord Care

questions.stem: A nurse is providing perineal care instructions to a postpartum client. Which instruction is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Apply ice directly to the perineum without a protective barrier or cloth between the ice and skin","B":"Wipe from front to back, and use a peri-bottle with warm water after voiding to promote comfort and hygiene","C":"Avoid all perineal hygiene entirely for the first week postpartum to protect the healing tissue","D":"Wipe from back to front after voiding or defecating, then pat the area dry with a clean towel"}}
questions.rationale: Postpartum perineal care includes wiping front to back to reduce infection risk, and using a peri-bottle with warm water after voiding or defecating to gently cleanse the area and promote comfort, particularly important with any perineal trauma or episiotomy.
questions.source_name: AWHONN — Postpartum Perineal Care Guidelines

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client in the third trimester of pregnancy who is lying supine for an ultrasound and suddenly reports dizziness, lightheadedness, and nausea. The nurse's priority action is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reposition the client onto her left side to relieve pressure the gravid uterus is placing on the vena cava","B":"Encourage the client to sit up rapidly, reasoning that the dizziness is unrelated to her current supine positioning","C":"Elevate only the client's legs while keeping her positioned flat on her back throughout the procedure","D":"Have the client remain flat on her back and simply wait for the symptoms to resolve on their own"}}
questions.rationale: In late pregnancy, the gravid uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when a client lies supine, reducing venous return and causing supine hypotensive syndrome. Repositioning to the left lateral position relieves this pressure and is the priority intervention.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Maternal Positioning in Pregnancy
questions.source_detail: Supine Hypotensive Syndrome and Left Lateral Positioning

questions.stem: When giving a bed bath to a client, the nurse should generally wash the body in which order?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"From the feet upward to the face, working against the usual clean-to-dirty sequence","B":"From the cleanest area (such as the face) to the least clean area (such as the perineal area) last","C":"In a random order based on staff convenience, with no particular clean-to-dirty sequence","D":"From the perineal area first, then moving upward to wash the face at the very end"}}
questions.rationale: Standard bed bath technique follows a clean-to-dirty principle, generally starting with the face/eyes (cleanest area) and moving toward the perineal area (least clean) last, using separate sections of the washcloth or fresh water as needed to minimize cross-contamination.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Bed Bath Technique

questions.stem: A nurse is providing postpartum follow-up care six weeks after delivery and screens the client for depression using a validated tool, even though the client reports feeling "basically fine." This practice reflects:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A screening that is considered most relevant during pregnancy itself, with frequency typically decreasing after delivery","B":"A screening best deferred to a mental health specialist rather than incorporated into routine postpartum nursing visits like this one","C":"A lower-priority screening, since most postpartum mood changes are assumed to resolve without any formal intervention","D":"Standard, recommended practice at this stage of care, since low mood may not be obvious even when someone reports feeling okay, and early support matters"}}
questions.rationale: Routine screening for postpartum depression using validated tools (such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) is a recommended standard practice, since postpartum depression is common, often underrecognized, and benefits significantly from timely identification and treatment.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Screening for Perinatal Depression

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a new mother about proper breastfeeding latch technique. Which observation indicates a correct latch?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The infant's lips are tucked inward, with only the tip of the nipple in the mouth","B":"The infant's mouth covers a large portion of the areola, with lips flanged outward","C":"The infant's chin is pulled away from the breast throughout most of the feeding","D":"The mother reports persistent, sharp nipple pain that continues throughout the entire feeding"}}
questions.rationale: A correct breastfeeding latch involves the infant taking a large portion of the areola (not just the nipple) into the mouth, with lips flanged outward, chin touching the breast, and should not cause persistent sharp pain, which often indicates an improper latch needing correction.
questions.source_name: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine — Proper Latch Technique

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion teaching about cervical cancer screening. The nurse should explain that Pap smear screening intervals are generally based on:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A fixed screening schedule applied identically to every client with no individual variation","B":"Only a family history of unrelated, non-gynecologic cancers, with no other factor considered","C":"The client's age and individual risk factors, per current guidelines","D":"Only the client's own personal preference, with no clinical guideline informing the decision"}}
questions.rationale: Cervical cancer (Pap smear) screening recommendations are based on age and individual risk factors, with intervals varying accordingly per current guidelines (such as those from ACOG and USPSTF), and clients should discuss their personalized screening schedule with their provider.
questions.source_name: ACOG / USPSTF — Cervical Cancer Screening Guidelines

questions.stem: A postpartum client reports mild mood swings and tearfulness that began two days after delivery and resolved within two weeks without any treatment, and the client's partner asks whether this means something is seriously wrong. The nurse should recognize this as most consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Postpartum depression, a condition that would require immediate initiation of antidepressant medication","B":"Postpartum (\"baby\") blues, a common, typically self-limited experience that resolves on its own, as happened here","C":"Postpartum psychosis, a condition requiring immediate emergency psychiatric hospitalization","D":"A definite sign of inadequate maternal-infant bonding requiring urgent intervention"}}
questions.rationale: Postpartum blues are common, typically mild, and self-limited, usually resolving within two weeks without treatment. This differs from postpartum depression, which is more persistent, severe, and requires clinical intervention, and from postpartum psychosis, a rare, severe psychiatric emergency.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Postpartum Blues vs. Postpartum Depression

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a family experiencing a perinatal loss (stillbirth), and a well-meaning colleague suggests it may be easier for the family if contact with the infant is kept to a minimum. An appropriate nursing intervention instead is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Structure care to limit the family's contact with the infant, based on the belief that distance from the loss eases grieving over time, as the colleague suggested","B":"Offer the family the opportunity to see and hold the infant if desired, and provide compassionate, individualized bereavement support","C":"Avoid direct discussion of the loss with the family, in order to reduce the risk of causing them additional emotional distress","D":"Arrange for a shorter length of stay than the family might otherwise want, in order to minimize their time on the unit following the loss"}}
questions.rationale: Compassionate perinatal bereavement care includes offering families the opportunity (not obligation) to see, hold, and create memories with their infant if desired, along with individualized emotional support, since these practices are associated with better grief processing for many families.
questions.source_name: Perinatal Bereavement Care Standards — Compassionate Care for Perinatal Loss

questions.stem: A laboring client's family requests specific cultural practices during childbirth, including a particular birthing position and the presence of an extended family member, both of which differ from routine hospital protocol. The nurse's most appropriate response is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ignore the family's request altogether and proceed with the standard unit routine as usual for every client","B":"Deny the request outright, explaining that hospital routine must be maintained without exception in every case","C":"Assess the requested practices for safety and, whenever safely possible, accommodate the family's specific cultural practices","D":"Assume this family wants the exact same practices as every other family from a similar cultural background entirely"}}
questions.rationale: Culturally sensitive maternity care involves assessing specific requests for safety and, whenever safely and practically possible, accommodating the family's cultural and personal preferences during childbirth, supporting a positive, respectful birth experience.
questions.source_name: AWHONN — Culturally Competent Maternity Care

questions.stem: A provider orders a heparin infusion based on a weight-based protocol for a client with a pulmonary embolism, and a newer nurse asks why the dose isn't just a standard fixed rate like some other medications. The nurse understands that weight-based dosing is used for heparin because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Heparin has a narrow therapeutic index, and weight-based dosing helps achieve a more predictable, therapeutic anticoagulant effect for this client","B":"Heparin's distribution throughout the body is only modestly related to weight, making it a relatively minor factor in dosing decisions","C":"Weight-based dosing is primarily a convenience for simplifying the nurse's calculations, rather than being tied to actual therapeutic drug levels","D":"Heparin has a wide therapeutic window that makes precise weight-based calculation less clinically important for this medication"}}
questions.rationale: Heparin has a narrow therapeutic index and significant inter-patient variability in response. Weight-based dosing protocols help achieve more predictable therapeutic anticoagulation while reducing the risk of under- or over-anticoagulation compared to fixed dosing.
questions.source_name: ACCP (American College of Chest Physicians) — Heparin Dosing Guidelines

questions.stem: A client starting warfarin therapy is also receiving a heparin infusion for several days, and the client asks the nurse why two different blood thinners are needed at once. The nurse understands this "bridging" approach is used because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The heparin infusion alone is sufficient to allow less frequent INR monitoring during this early transition period between drugs","B":"The two medications are generally avoided in combination, since they are thought to interact unpredictably when given together like this","C":"Warfarin is expected to produce a measurable anticoagulant effect within the first hour or two following the client's initial dose","D":"Warfarin takes several days to reach a therapeutic effect, so the heparin provides anticoagulation during this transition period until warfarin takes full effect"}}
questions.rationale: Warfarin takes several days to achieve a therapeutic anticoagulant effect because it works by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis. Heparin is often used as a "bridge" to provide immediate anticoagulation until the INR reaches the therapeutic range, at which point heparin is discontinued.
questions.source_name: ACCP — Anticoagulation Bridging Therapy Guidelines

questions.stem: A client taking a beta-blocker for hypertension and a history of stable angina wants to stop the medication because they feel it is unnecessary now that their blood pressure readings look good. The nurse should explain that abruptly stopping this medication can cause:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An immediate, sustained improvement in the client's blood pressure control would be expected once this medication is stopped this way today","B":"Rebound hypertension and potentially tachycardia or angina, due to abrupt discontinuation, which is a particular concern given this client's angina history","C":"A guaranteed allergic reaction would be expected to develop within hours of stopping this medication so abruptly like this","D":"No significant physiologic effect at all would be expected from stopping this particular type of medication so abruptly"}}
questions.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation of beta-blockers can cause a rebound effect, including rebound hypertension, tachycardia, and potentially angina or myocardial infarction in susceptible clients, due to upregulated beta-receptor sensitivity during chronic therapy. These medications should be tapered gradually under provider guidance.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Beta-Blockers

questions.stem: A client taking clonidine for hypertension misses several doses while traveling and calls the clinic reporting a pounding headache and a blood pressure reading at home that is much higher than usual. The nurse should recognize the risk of which effect from this abrupt discontinuation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Bradycardia by itself, with fairly little accompanying blood pressure effect, despite the client's reported home reading today","B":"Hypotension, an effect essentially opposite to what this client's home blood pressure reading actually shows right now","C":"Little significant effect worth mentioning, despite the client's reported headache and elevated home blood pressure reading today","D":"Rebound hypertension, potentially severe, which is consistent with this client's elevated home reading and headache after missing several doses"}}
questions.rationale: Clonidine, a centrally-acting antihypertensive, carries a well-documented risk of rebound hypertension (sometimes severe) with abrupt discontinuation, due to a surge in sympathetic activity. This medication should be tapered gradually rather than stopped suddenly.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Clonidine
questions.source_detail: Warnings: Rebound Hypertension with Abrupt Discontinuation

questions.stem: A client taking digoxin is newly prescribed verapamil for hypertension. The nurse should recognize this combination as significant because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Verapamil substantially decreases digoxin absorption, effectively eliminating its therapeutic effect","B":"Verapamil can increase digoxin levels, raising the risk of digoxin toxicity","C":"Verapamil has no pharmacokinetic interaction with digoxin whatsoever in this combination","D":"This particular drug combination carries no clinical significance worth monitoring for"}}
questions.rationale: Verapamil can increase serum digoxin concentrations through pharmacokinetic interactions, raising the risk of digoxin toxicity. Close monitoring of digoxin levels and toxicity signs is warranted when these medications are used together, and dose adjustment may be needed.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Digoxin Drug Interactions

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing medications for an 84-year-old client and notes a new prescription for a sedating first-generation antihistamine, such as diphenhydramine, for occasional allergy symptoms. The nurse should recognize a particular concern in this client due to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An increased risk of sedation, confusion, and falls in older adults, given this medication's known anticholinergic and sedating effects in this population","B":"An enhanced therapeutic effect with fewer side effects would typically be expected in older adults taking this medication class overall","C":"Improved cognitive function is often associated with this particular medication class when it is given to older clients like this one","D":"No specific concerns exist in older adults at all, despite this medication's well-documented risks in this particular client population"}}
questions.rationale: Sedating first-generation antihistamines are included on lists of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults (such as the Beers Criteria) due to increased anticholinergic effects, sedation, confusion, and significantly increased fall risk in this population.
questions.source_name: American Geriatrics Society — Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medications

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to use a newly prescribed inhaled corticosteroid for asthma. Which instruction helps prevent a common local adverse effect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Skip rinsing the mouth after each use, since this step offers no meaningful clinical benefit","B":"Rinse the mouth with water after each use to reduce the risk of oral thrush (candidiasis)","C":"Use the inhaler only once per week, regardless of the client's actual symptom frequency","D":"Avoid using a spacer device with the inhaler, since it reduces medication delivery to the lungs"}}
questions.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause local deposition in the oropharynx, increasing the risk of oral thrush (candidiasis). Rinsing the mouth with water (and spitting it out) after each use, along with using a spacer device when appropriate, helps reduce this risk.
questions.source_name: GINA (Global Initiative for Asthma) — Inhaled Corticosteroid Use Guidance
questions.source_detail: Oral Thrush Prevention with Inhaled Corticosteroids

questions.stem: A client uses an insulin pump for continuous subcutaneous insulin delivery and mentions leaving the same infusion site in place for over a week because it "still seems to be working fine." The nurse should teach the client that a key safety consideration with pump therapy is:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular site rotation and monitoring for signs of infusion set malfunction, which can cause rapid hyperglycemia or DKA if delivery is interrupted","B":"Less frequent monitoring for hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia is appropriate once the initial pump programming has been verified as accurate","C":"A reduced, manageable risk of major glucose excursions develops once the pump has been functioning correctly for several days","D":"Reliable function for extended periods can be expected without routine site rotation or infusion set troubleshooting actually being necessary"}}
questions.rationale: Because insulin pumps typically deliver only rapid-acting insulin, an interruption in delivery (from a kinked or dislodged infusion set, for example) can lead to rapid hyperglycemia and risk of DKA, since there is no long-acting insulin "on board." Regular site rotation, monitoring, and troubleshooting knowledge are essential safety components of pump therapy.
questions.source_name: ADA — Insulin Pump Therapy Education Standards
questions.source_detail: Safety Considerations for Insulin Pump Therapy

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer an opioid to a client who has never previously taken opioids ("opioid-naive") for acute post-surgical pain, and a colleague suggests using the same dose given to a client down the hall who takes opioids chronically for cancer pain. Compared to that opioid-tolerant client, the nurse should recognize that this opioid-naive client:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Requires a lower starting dose and closer monitoring for respiratory depression, since tolerance has not developed the way it has for the other client","B":"Should be given a somewhat higher starting dose to compensate for this client's lack of prior opioid exposure","C":"Should be started at the same dose typically reserved for a client with an established, ongoing opioid tolerance, as the colleague suggested","D":"Should be monitored at the same baseline frequency used for a client with a well-established tolerance profile"}}
questions.rationale: Opioid-naive clients have not developed pharmacologic tolerance to opioids, making them more susceptible to respiratory depression at doses that opioid-tolerant clients might tolerate well. Lower starting doses and closer monitoring are standard practice for opioid-naive clients.
questions.source_name: FDA — Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) Education

questions.stem: A nurse is providing education about a newly prescribed SSRI antidepressant for a 15-year-old client, and the parent asks whether there is anything specific they should watch for at home. Which safety information is essential to include, per the FDA boxed warning for this medication class?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"There is an increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults, especially early in treatment, requiring close monitoring","B":"SSRIs carry no notable psychiatric risk when prescribed to a client in this particular age group, unlike what the boxed warning states","C":"The medication should be discontinued immediately at the very first sign of any side effect the client happens to experience","D":"This medication class is considered appropriate for use only in an older adult population, rather than in adolescents like this client"}}
questions.rationale: FDA labeling includes a boxed warning that antidepressants, including SSRIs, are associated with an increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults, particularly during the initial months of treatment or with dose changes, requiring close monitoring.
questions.source_name: FDA — Boxed Warning for Antidepressants in Pediatric and Young Adult Populations
